title: Typed tool-call interop shims and graceful backoff patterns
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Build cross-language helpers for function/tool calling that provide: (1) runtime schema validation with helpful errors, (2) ergonomic typed bindings for TypeScript/Python/Go, (3) a single configurable backoff/retry policy that supports both unary and streaming invocations, and (4) resume-friendly streaming adapters for long-running tool outputs. The goal is to reduce customer friction when wiring model function outputs to application code while keeping failure semantics predictable and observable. Work includes API surface design, compatibility layer for older SDK versions, performance testing, and documenting migration patterns.
acceptance_criteria: - SDKs expose a consistent TypedToolCall helper in TS/Python/Go.
notes: Motivation: customers keep implementing ad-hoc schema coercion and duplicate retry logic in examples and sent PRs with fragile stream parsing.

Key outcomes: reduce parsing errors by >40% in example-app telemetry; provide a single retry policy that respects streaming partials and per-token progress; ensure TypeScript types align with runtime validation for developer ergonomics.
design_decisions: Use JSON Schema (subset) for function arg validation but limit to shape/type checks — avoid full $ref resolution to reduce bundle size in TS clients.
Expose two layers: validateAndCall (strict, throws) and coerceAndCall (best-effort coercions with warnings).
Retry policy: exponential backoff with jitter, max attempts configurable per-route; streaming retries will attempt a transparent resume only if tool supports idempotent range tokens (protocol-level).
Telemetry: emit events for validation failures, retry attempts, resume attempts, and final outcome with token counts.
tradeoffs: Bundle size vs validation power: lightweight validator chosen for browser and edge SDKs at cost of fewer advanced schema features.
Automatic stream resume complexity: adding transparent resume increases server requirements (token checkpoints); we default to explicit resume API to reduce server-side coupling.
Strict validation may break existing users who rely on coercion; provide coerce mode to ease migration.
implementation_plan: 1) Design TS public API and runtime validator (PoC) — DUE 2026-03-05
2) Implement Python shim with pydantic-lite validator and streaming adapter — DUE 2026-03-09
3) Implement Go interfaces and type helpers; ensure zero-copy for common cases — DUE 2026-03-12
4) Cross-SDK e2e tests using internal echo-tool and flaky-network simulator — DUE 2026-03-13
5) Docs, migration guide, and example app updates — DUE 2026-03-15
progress_updates: 2026-03-02: Initial API proposal reviewed by SDK PMs (shared in Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SDK/Typed+Tool+Call+Proposal). Feedback requested on coerce mode semantics.

2026-03-04: TS PoC completed: runtime validator (60KB uncompressed) + typed wrapper. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/4123. Found two edge cases around nullable arrays — added spec note.

2026-03-06: Python shim prototype demonstrates pydantic-lite coercion and strict modes. Benchmarked validation overhead: ~0.45ms per call on small payloads. Open issue created: ENG-96410 for optimizing validator caching.

2026-03-07: Implemented streaming adapter prototype; decided to support explicit resume tokens in first iteration instead of transparent resume to simplify infra changes. Added acceptance criteria to require resume token handshake in tool contract.
review_feedback: Design review (2026-03-03) from SDK lead: prefer validator plugin approach so customers can opt into full ajv in server builds.
Security review request queued — need to validate that coerce mode does not silently accept dangerous payloads (sensitive fields).
Performance review: go SDK should avoid allocation in hot path; Marco to add zero-allocation benchmarks.
communication_plan: Post RFC to SDK weekly sync and include migration notes for early adopters.
Notify Solutions Engineering channel with example migration PRs.
Blog/internal notes summarizing tradeoffs once feature gates landed.
risks: Misalignment between runtime validation and static types leading to confusing developer errors.
Too-large runtime validator increases browser bundle sizes and may discourage adoption.
Streaming resume requires server-side contract changes; rolling back is non-trivial.
